THOUGHT: This 28-year-old male presents with acute-onset dizziness, palpitations, fatigue, and exertional dyspnea over the past 2 days, following a bout of heavy alcohol consumption at a bachelor party. His vital signs reveal an irregularly irregular heart rate (88–110 bpm), and physical exam shows no signs of heart failure (no JVD, no edema, no murmurs). The ECG is diagnostic: absent P waves, irregularly irregular R-R intervals — classic for atrial fibrillation (AFib). Laboratory evaluation rules out common secondary causes: electrolyte abnormalities, thyroid dysfunction (e.g., hyperthyroidism), anemia, and active intoxication (alcohol level now normal). Given his age, absence of structural heart disease (no murmurs, no signs of cardiomyopathy or valvular disease), and clear temporal association with binge alcohol intake, this is highly consistent with “holiday heart syndrome” — a well-described entity of acute, often self-limited AFib triggered by acute alcohol exposure in otherwise healthy individuals. While other arrhythmias (e.g., multifocal atrial tachycardia, atrial flutter with variable block) can mimic AFib, the ECG findings are unequivocal for AFib. No evidence supports alternative diagnoses such as pheochromocytoma (no episodic hypertension, headache, diaphoresis), anxiety disorder (objective ECG and clinical findings confirm arrhythmia), or vestibular dizziness (neurologic exam normal, dizziness is associated with palpitations and exertional dyspnea — suggesting hemodynamic consequence of arrhythmia).

DIAGNOSIS: Alcohol-induced atrial fibrillation
